prompt: What does the lesson say separates PRINCE2 from the PMBOK Guide?

choices.text: PRINCE2 has no principles, only a long list of required documents
choices.why: It has seven principles, and they define it.
It is used for projects of every kind.
Right. It says who does what, in which process, producing which document.
It is the British government's method.

prompt: A project's business case stops making sense in stage three. What does PRINCE2's first principle require?

choices.why: Right. The justification is checked at every stage, and a project without one is stopped.

choices.text: Rewrite the business case to fit the project as it is now
choices.why: That inverts the principle.

choices.text: Carry on; the case was approved at the start
choices.why: It must stay valid, not merely have been valid.

choices.text: Finish the stage and then decide what to do
choices.why: The principle exists to stop the money going in.

prompt: Match each Project Board role to what it represents.

pairs.right: The business case, with the final say
The people who will use the output
The people who will build it

prompt: Is the Project Manager a member of the Project Board?

choices.why: The Executive has the final say, not the Project Manager.
The roles do not change by stage.
The Senior Supplier represents those who build.
Right. The board directs; the Project Manager manages day to day.

prompt: When must a PRINCE2 Project Manager raise an exception to the board?

choices.text: When a forecast says a tolerance will be exceeded
choices.why: Right. The board hears about it before it happens, with options.
Inside the tolerances the Project Manager decides alone.

choices.text: Every week, with a full status report
choices.why: Routine reports happen at set intervals; an exception is different.

choices.text: Only after a tolerance has been exceeded
choices.why: By then the board has lost the chance to act early.

prompt: Which of these are tolerances in the 2017 edition of PRINCE2? Choose all that apply.

choices.why: Not one of the six.
A Scrum practice, not a tolerance.
Yes.
Yes.
Yes.

prompt: A board sets every tolerance to zero. What does the lesson predict?
hint: Where would the board's attention go?

choices.text: The first exception arrives too late
choices.why: That is the failure of tolerances set too wide.

choices.text: The Project Manager gains more freedom
choices.why: The opposite: no room at all.

choices.text: Every small deviation becomes an exception
choices.why: Right. The board is consulted on everything and management by exception disappears.

choices.text: The project will never deviate from the plan, so nothing changes
choices.why: Zero tolerance does not prevent deviation; it only reports all of it.

prompt: Which Scrum element does the lesson compare with a PRINCE2 tolerance?
hint: Room to renegotiate inside a limit.

choices.why: Right. The Developers change the plan freely and bring the Product Owner in only when the goal is at risk.
A daily inspection, not a limit.

choices.text: The retrospective at the end of the Sprint
choices.why: It improves the process; it sets no tolerance.

choices.text: The burndown chart drawn by the team
choices.why: A chart of progress, not a delegated limit.

prompt: In PRINCE2 Agile, which tolerance is usually set wide?
hint: What does agile work expect to vary?

choices.why: Benefits are why the project exists; they are not where agile flexes.
Time is usually held tighter.
Cost is usually held tighter.
Right. Time and cost are held tighter: fixed date, variable scope.

prompt: Where does the lesson say an architect contributes in a PRINCE2 project? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: As Executive of the Project Board
choices.why: The Executive owns the business case for the organisation.
Yes: the cost and risk of the technical options.
Yes: the quality criteria.
Yes: technical assurance for the board.

prompt: Which board role does the lesson say an architect should work with?
hint: Who answers for whether it can be built?

choices.text: Nobody; architects work only with developers
choices.why: The lesson names a board role.
An administrative role, not on the board.
Right. The architect's assessment is the evidence that role brings to the board.

choices.text: The Senior User, who represents the people who will use the system
choices.why: Users, not builders.

prompt: Put RUP's four phases in order.
trap: Elaboration comes before construction: the architecture is proved before the rest is built on it.

prompt: What is the deliverable at the end of RUP's elaboration phase?

choices.text: The finished system, ready for users
choices.why: That comes at the end of transition.
That is a waterfall deliverable.
Right. The lifecycle architecture milestone: the riskiest parts built and measured.

choices.text: A complete UML model of every class in the system
choices.why: RUP uses models, but elaboration's milestone is running code.

prompt: What does the hump chart show that a waterfall diagram does not?

choices.text: That requirements are frozen after inception
choices.why: Requirements work continues, smaller.
It has four; the difference is what a phase contains.

choices.text: Every discipline in every phase, in different amounts
choices.why: Right. Testing runs throughout and there is implementation in elaboration.

choices.text: That testing happens only at the end
choices.why: The chart shows testing in every phase.

prompt: Kruchten's model describes an architecture with four views tied together by scenarios, and is known as the ___ view model.
What does the lesson say made RUP heavy in practice?
hint: It was a framework to select from.

choices.why: It was iterative by design.

choices.text: Organisations adopted far more of it than they needed
choices.why: Right. It was a failure to tailor; its authors said to select.
That is XP.
It had four.

prompt: Match each successor to what it kept from RUP.

pairs.right: The four phases with minimal artefacts
Inception, construction and transition around agile iterations
An architectural runway built ahead of features

prompt: Which idea from RUP does the lesson say an architect should keep?

choices.text: Buy the tools from one vendor
choices.why: The tie to tools worked against it.

choices.text: Write a document for every activity
choices.why: That is the heaviness that sank it.

choices.text: Prove the riskiest decisions in running code, early
choices.why: Right. A working skeleton is a set of tested decisions, which narrows the cone.

choices.text: Model every class in UML first
choices.why: Modelling is not the point the lesson keeps.

prompt: In the translation table, what is the nearest thing in a Scrum team to a PRINCE2 business case or a PMBOK charter?

choices.why: That is about quality, closer to product descriptions.
A daily inspection.

choices.text: The Sprint Backlog of the current Sprint
choices.why: A plan for one Sprint, not the reason for the project.
Right. Both say what the work is for.

prompt: You join a project run under PRINCE2 and want the riskiest integration proved early. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Ask for a stage whose deliverable is a working skeleton
choices.why: Right. Elaboration's idea, written as a PRINCE2 stage with a product description.

choices.text: Raise an exception before anything is built
choices.why: An exception is a forecast of exceeding tolerance, not a design request.
That leaves the risk where it is most expensive.

choices.text: Argue that the organisation should switch to Scrum
choices.why: Fighting the vocabulary is usually less effective than using it.

prompt: Which of the lesson's three questions tells you how expensive changing a design decision will be?
hint: Change control or the next planning session.

choices.why: Right. A change request with impact assessment costs more than the next planning session.
That tells you what evidence your work is judged by.

choices.text: Which method is the best one for the organisation?
choices.why: Not one of the three, and rarely a useful question.

choices.text: Who can stop the project, and when do they look?
choices.why: That tells you when a risk must be raised.

prompt: Which idea do PRINCE2's management by exception and Kanban's work-in-progress limit share, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Set a limit and act when it is about to be crossed
choices.why: Right. Both leave people free inside the limit.

choices.text: Plan the whole project up front
choices.why: Neither requires it.
PRINCE2 keeps four levels.

choices.text: Report everything to the level above
choices.why: Both exist to avoid that.

prompt: How many principles does PRINCE2 have?
hint: Three sets of the same number.
